Based on a comprehensive evaluation of the paper and reviewers' feedback, I recommend ​rejecting​ this submission. Below is the detailed justification structured around critical flaws that undermine its contributions:

1. Reviewer SpSd confirms the authors themselves acknowledge Contribution (1) (verifying axioms for Hamming/Jaccard) is trivial. Contribution (3) (axioms for Jaccard) replicates known properties, e.g., the triangle inequality was proven in Lipiak (1999) and Graigeria et al. (2018). The work ignores Gössgens et al. (2021), which established an axiomatic framework for classification metrics applicable to binary vectors. This omission misrepresents the novelty of the axiomatic approach (Reviewer FAAB).

2. Key axioms (Independent Symmetry, Zero-One Symmetry, Convergence speed) lack practical or theoretical motivation. Reviewer FAAB notes these are not established as universally desirable properties, yet the paper frames them as foundational without justification. Both distances have well-documented biases(e.g., poor performance under class imbalance). Ignoring this—while alternatives like Matthews Correlation Coefficient address it—invalidates claims of a "comprehensive analysis" (Reviewer FAAB).

This paper attempts to axiomatize well-studied distances but delivers trivial verification of known properties, omits foundational literature, and selects axioms arbitrarily. The rebuttal offered superficial fixes (e.g., moving citations) but failed to motivate axioms, address biases, or prove core theorems. Given the ​lack of novelty, weak motivation, and unresolved execution gaps, the paper does not meet NeurIPS standards. I endorse rejection.

author_final_remarks.value:
Thank you again for the constructive feedback and insightful discussions.

We hope we managed to convince you of the value of axiomatic characterizations of the Hamming and Jaccard distances. These two measures are used in a very wide range of applications, within and beyond machine learning. Hence, their better understanding can be invaluable, and axiomatic characterization is a well-established tool to provide that. Among other benefits, it can guide the design of new, better-suited measures. We illustrate this in Section 5 of our work.

Based on the feedback received, we plan to incorporate the following changes in the revised version:
- Extend the related work section, including a comparison to the Gösgens et al. paper, as well as other papers analyzing related measures through the lens of properties they satisfy. We will also emphasize that certain properties of the Hamming and Jaccard distance, such as the triangle inequality, have already been shown.
- Add a table of which other measures from the literature satisfy which of our axioms.
- Expand the discussion on the motivation of our axioms by noting in which applications they are desirable and in which they are not.

We believe these changes will address the reviewers’ main concerns.

Thank you for considering our response in detail!

Let us explain our reasoning that led us to believe that Constant Baseline might not be particular important for the application of analysing approval election data.

There are (at least) two approaches one can have to such analysis. We can call them popularity-endorsing and popularity-invariant.

In the popularity-endorsing variant, we take the popularity of candidates into account when we decide whether they are similar or not. So, we might say, for example, that two candidates are quite similar, because they are both very unpopular (let say are supported by less than 1% of the voters), even if the sets of the supporters are not intersecting. In particular, they are more similar than one of them and any possible popular candidate (let say with more than 30% of voters supporting it). This is clearly contradicting Constant Baseline, as we explicitly say that against a very imbalanced vector, any similarly imbalanced vector will give lower dissimilarity score than any more balanced vector. Hence, Constant Baseline seem even undesirable in this case.

In the popularity-invariant version, we would like to be blind to the popularity of the candidates, and establish the connection based solely on other (latent) characteristics of the candidates. For example, in the political elections, we would like to capture a similarity between two left/right-wing candidates, even if one of them is very recognizable (and thus has a lot of supporters) and the other is quite niche (with very little supporters). Here, one could potentially make a case for Constant Baseline, but it still not very clear how exactly important it is. We observed that for this variant, it is crucial to recognize two candidates as very similar if the supporters of one of them form a subset of the supporters of the other (as this is likely to be the case of niche and popular candidates of the same leaning). However, it may turn out, that by imposing it (together with some other properties), we will loose Constant Baseline, as candidates that have low support, have higher chance of their supporters forming a subset of supporters of another candidate. But we would still choose a measure that finds such subset-of-supporters connections, over a measure that does not, but satisfies Constant Baseline. All in all, in our view, in this case, Constant Baseline may be a “nice-to-have” property, but we would not say it is crucial.

In our view, the main reason why Constant Baseline is a key property in the classification setting, but not so much in our applications, is that in the classification setting it serves as an incentive compatibility constraint. If it is not satisfied, the model can, in a certain sense, “cheat”, by producing imbalanced outputs, and in this way artificially increase its score (having more or less the same expertise level). However, the situation like that is not present in our setting. The data we analyse is given, and we do not evaluate its source. It may be that the fact that unpopular candidates are more similar to other candidates is just an inherent trait of the particular problem we are dealing with, and there is no direct disadvantage of that.

> For example, their Constant Baseline property, does not seem to be particularly important for the application we explore in Section 6, i.e., analysing approval election data.

In this case, it can be insightful to elaborate on that subject in the revised version of the text: for which of the considered applications such biases can be problematic or not. For instance, the absence of the constant baseline property can be not so problematic if one does not expect any imbalance in data or more problematic otherwise.

Let me briefly consider the election analysis application from Section 6. If I understand correctly, here you use the considered measures to evaluate the similarity of candidates given the vectors that describe who voted for these candidates. In this case, if some measure is biased towards the majority class (i.e., towards “no-vote”), then less popular candidates (with many 0s in their vectors) will be closer to other candidates (on average) than more popular ones just because of this bias. I think that in some applications of election analysis such behavior can potentially be undesirable.

Thank you for your work and discussion!

Thank you for the response to our rebuttal.

Let us briefly comment on your points.
1. Since we did not see our paper as primarily about classification, this bias did not strike us as a critical information to include in the paper. However, we will add it to the discussion in the revised version.
2. We see most of our axioms as potentially desirable in various situations, and not necessarily desirable, or even undesirable in others. 3. As already mentioned, Gösgens et al. had a clear focus on classification, and as such considered some axioms that are specific to that setting. For example, their _Constant Baseline_ property, does not seem to be particularly important for the application we explore in Section 6, i.e., analysing approval election data. Nevertheless, we agree that a more thorough literature review would be beneficial, and we thank the reviewer again for pointing us to this paper.
4. This is a very foundational research oriented paper, and us such it is difficult to clearly identify its direct impact, as the main goal is to deepen the understanding of the basic concepts. We hope that our results can help identify suitable measures and guide the development of new ones, the possibility of which we signal in Section 5. We are glad that the reviewer finds such papers as interesting and useful.

Thank you for your response! Based on the responses to all the reviewers, I better understand now what you consider to be the main contribution of the paper. I agree that while proving that the considered measures satisfy the properties can be easy, the task of finding the set of independent axioms that characterize the measures can be non-trivial. I appreciate this theoretical contribution of the work.

The points I am concerned about are:

1) Limited discussion of the negative aspects of the considered measures

It is widely known that these two measures have certain limitations. While there is some discussion on their limitations in the text, it is far from complete. For instance, arguably the most well-known and critical limitation is the bias of the measures when labels are unbalanced. This shortcoming is not discussed.

2) Limited discussion on the usefulness of properties

The main contribution of the paper is the set of independent axioms that characterize the measures. As I understand, this is the main motivation for choosing this particular set of axioms. However, the text of the paper can be misleading and may suggest that these properties are, in general, desirable. 

I think that it is important to discuss, for each property, whether it is universally desirable, or desirable in some cases, or formulated in this form just to obtain a suitable set of axioms.

3) Limited contextualization of the work within the existing literature

I believe it is important to perform a thorough review of related papers, many of which analyzed the considered measures. Gösgens et al. (2021) is only one example that I consider to be the most relevant.

> The main premise of the Gösgens et al. (2021) paper is to compare a large number of indices in order to find the most suitable ones for a quite specific application of evaluating classification performance

As far as I understand, all binary measures and all the properties analyzed in Gösgens et al. (2021) apply to the setup and distances considered in this work.

4) Potential impact

While I agree that the obtained result is theoretically interesting, its potential impact on some of the machine learning applications is not clear.

To sum up, I really appreciate the theoretical analysis conducted by the authors, and I find the papers of this type both interesting and useful. However, I believe that the submitted paper can be significantly improved, at least in the aspects of positioning, contextualization, and motivation.

Thank you for your response.

(B) The Hamming and Jaccard distances are widely used in many different applications (within and beyond machine learning), thus we believe that better understanding them through the lens of axiomatic characterization can be very valuable. One of the potential benefits is that it can guide the development of new measures, for which we give an example in Section 5 of our paper.

The quoted sentence is also important. For instance, based on the axiomatic differences we have identified, it seems that Jaccard is more suitable to applications where the vectors are sparse (because of the Add Zero axiom, which is desirable in such situations), while Hamming is a better choice when the role of 0s and 1s is symmetric (by Zero-One Symmetry), which might be the case, e.g., when we want to assess binary classification model, in which there is no objective preference between the labels (for example, for predicting the outcomes of sport events).

(C) The two sentences that the reviewer is quoting refer to the axiomatic characterization results (we say there that these measures are **unique** ones to satisfy the respective axioms). We assumed that the fact that the Jaccard distance satisfies the triangle inequality is widely known, and this is why we do not need to be very upfront about the fact that it has been shown before (and as we said, we do not claim that this fact, or any fact that the distances satisfy some of our axioms, is an important contribution of our paper). However, based on the comment from the reviewer, to make it definitely clear, we will move the references for the satisfaction of the triangle inequality by Jaccard to the main body of the paper.

We thank the reviewer for the feedback and the concern raised. However, we respectfully believe that they are not fully justified, which we explain below.

A.
While proving that the Hamming distance satisfies all axioms that characterize it is indeed not very difficult, we would like to point out that obtaining the set of independent axioms that provide the characterization is a highly non-trivial task.

B.
In this point, the reviewer is questioning the value and usefulness of the very concept of an axiomatic characterization, which is a well established tool for understanding various concepts in machine learning and mathematical sciences in general. Let us provide some arguments defending it.

* First, an axiomatic characterization provides better understanding of the studied measure. It can be seen as an alternative definition of the measure that stems from its properties, which gives valuable intuition on where this particular measure is coming from.
* Second, an axiomatic characterization shows that the set of axioms that are considered is, in certain sense, complete. One can propose many different properties that a measure may satisfy, but the characterization result (together with the independence result) provides a justification for a very specific set of such properties.
* Every axiomatic characterization is at the same time an impossibility result, saying that there cannot be a measure satisfying a given set of properties, and at the same time satisfy a property not satisfied by the characterized measure. This shows certain inherent trade-off between the properties.
* Axiomatic characterization of two different measures that share many common axioms, allow for capturing the key differences and similarities between the studied measures. In our case, we identify a key difference between Hamming and Jaccard, which can explain why they may be better suited for different settings. 
* Finally, axiomatic characterizations can guide the choice and development of new measures. With additional information on which axioms are the most desirable and which are not crucial (or even undesirable), we can design new measures that purposefully preserve some axioms and drop the others. An example of such analysis is conducted in Section 5 of our paper.


C.
We have acknowledged the existing proofs of the fact that the Jaccard distance satisfies the triangle inequality (line 862) and in general, similarly to the case for the Hamming distance, we do not claim that proving that the Jaccard distance satisfies the respective set of axioms is difficult (see lines 168–169, which are analogous to line 122 mentioned by the reviewer).  What is challenging is (1) designing the set of axioms that characterize the Jaccard distance in a way that large part of the axioms coincide with the axioms used for the characterization of Hamming, and (2) proving that the only measure satisfying these axioms is the Jaccard distance.

D.
We are quite surprised by this comment since the formal statement of Theorem 4.2 is presented in lines 165–166.

We thank the reviewer for the feedback and insightful comments.

We also thank for pointing us to the Gösgens et al. (2021) paper. While it is related to our work, and we will mention it and compare to it in the final version of our paper, we would like to point out that there are important differences in the goals and methods of both papers.

The main premise of the Gösgens et al. (2021) paper is to compare a large number of indices in order to find the most suitable ones for a quite specific application of evaluating classification performance. In contrast, in our work we strive to provide a better understanding of two very specific dissimilarity measures, but widely popular across many different applications (within and beyond machine learning), i.e., the Hamming and Jaccard distances.

For this reason, we do not limit ourselves to only analysing which properties are satisfied by which measure, but provide an axiomatic characterizations of both considered metrics. This in part guides our choice of the set of considered axioms and shows the completeness of that set.

The fact that the goal is to understand rather than to find the best is also why not all of the properties discussed by us are necessarily desired in some of the potential applications. In fact, in Section 5, this is exactly our point: there, we show that a property that is satisfied by both Hamming and Jaccard, namely Independent Symmetry, is undesirable in certain settings. As a result, we provide another argument why these very popular measures should be sometimes avoided, akin to the known biases which the reviewer has mentioned.

Nevertheless, for each of our axioms, there is a large number of popular measures that satisfy it (see some examples in the response to reviewer ZKPf).

The extension of our analysis to more complex measures, with potentially better properties, is a very promising direction for the future work. However, we strongly believe that the first step should be to establish a good axiomatic understanding of the most basic and most popular measures.

Another, issue that we would like to clarify is the usage of the word “axiom”.  This term is quite commonly used to describe properties characterizing certain concepts in machine learning (see e.g., Ackerman, Ben-David, A Characterization of Linkage-Based Hierarchical Clustering, 2016, or Sebastiani, An axiomatically derived measure for the evaluation of classification algorithms, 2015), game theory (e.g.,  Shapley, A value for n-person games, 1953), and many other areas.

Furthermore, we would like to defend the axiom of Zero-One Symmetry, which the reviewer dismissed as not motivated. As we have written in the paper, in certain settings, the labels of one and zero are assigned arbitrarily and play symmetric role. For instance, this is the case in some of the applications of binary classification, in which the outcomes are completely symmetric and there is no objective valuation between the labels.  For example, consider predicting sport event outcomes or distinguishing between two classes of objects based on their picture (e.g., truck vs standard car). Then, if we want to be truly impartial, we should assume that what we assign to the value of zero and what to the value of one does not change the value of the metric. And this is exactly what Zero-One Symmetry is formalizing.

Finally, let us answer the questions posed by the reviewer.

Q: Can different clustering algorithms change the results in Section 6.2?

A: We have tried different clustering algorithms: for some, the results were similar, for some the clusters were less intuitive for all considered measures, which is more due to properties of the clustering method than our measures. In the paper, we focused on the average-based hierarchical clustering, as it is arguably one of the simplest and most basic clustering methods. We can include some additional results with other clustering algorithms in the final version of the paper.

Q: What is the motivation for clustering 2D-Euclidean data generated through uniform distribution of points?

A: Although indeed there is no ground-truth clustering in the data we generate, there is still a very strong structure in the data that corresponds to the spatial distribution of the candidates. We use clustering to check whether our measures can recover this underlying structure.

The assumption that the distribution of candidates is uniform intuitively makes the clustering task the hardest possible. If we considered candidates generated with a mixture of k Gaussians, for example, the task would be easier overall, but we expect the performance of the measures to be similar.

Observe that this task is a certain abstraction of the task of clustering projects in the participatory budgeting setting, where the voters are more likely to support projects which are closer to them. It is then probably not a coincidence that a measure that performed well in this experiment, i.e., geometric Jaccard, also was the most correlated with the distance between the physical locations of projects in real-world participatory budgeting instances (see Table 4 in Section 6.3).

Thank you for the insightful review and support for our work!

Let us respond to each of your questions.

Q: Which axioms p-Hamming and p-Jaccard satisfy?

A: Every p-Hamming, for p different than 1, satisfies Anonymity, Scaling, Zero-One Symmetry, Convergence, and Normalization, but fails Independent Symmetry. Similarly, every p-Jaccard, for p different than 1, satisfies Anonymity, Scaling, Convergence, Normalization, and Add Zero, but fails Independent Symmetry.

Q: Which axioms are satisfied by other distances such as Dice index, Tversky index, and Sympson's overlap coefficient?

A: While these distances are not as standard and popular as the Hamming and Jaccard distance, we agree that it might be useful to provide information which axioms they satisfy. Thank you for the suggestion! We will include such comparison in the final version of our work (which will include the measures you mentioned as well as others).

The distance based on Dice index (i.e., 1 minus Dice index) satisfies Anonymity, Scaling, Independent Symmetry, Convergence, Normalization, and Add Zero, but fails Zero-One Symmetry and Triangle Inequality.

The distance based on Sympson's overlap coefficient (again, 1 minus the coefficient) satisfies Anonymity, Scaling, Convergence, Normalization, and Add Zero, but fails Independent Symmetry,  Zero-One Symmetry, and Triangle Inequality.

Tversky’s index gives us a whole family of measures including Jaccard and Dice index, so for particular values of parameters the exact set of satisfied axioms might differ. However, every measure in the family necessarily satisfies Anonymity, Scaling, Convergence, Normalization, and Add Zero.

Thank you for the insightful review and support for our work!

Let us respond to each of your questions.

Q: What does ‘saturation’ mean in line 42?

A: Throughout the paper by ‘saturation’ we mean the number of ones in the vector divided by the length of the vector. What we say in this sentence is that two vectors with significantly different number of ones are usually considered as very distant from each other by measures that satisfy Independent Symmetry (even if the indices on which one of the vectors has ones form a subset of such indices of the other vector). We will clarify that in the final version.

Q: What does 'except for this one' mean in the statements of Theorems 3.9 and 4.3.

A: In both theorems, we consider a set of axioms with which we characterize either Hamming or Jaccard distance. We show that for every axiom $A$ in such a set of axioms $X$, there exists a dissimilarity measure $f$ that does not satisfy axiom $A$, but satisfies every axiom $A' \in X$ distinct from $A$. The term 'this one' in the phrase in question refers to axiom $A$, which is not satisfied.

Q: Can the assumptions of Proposition 6.1 be relaxed?

A: We can understand the inclusion of unordered rows as introducing noise to our model of 1D-Euclidean data. Then, it is natural, that as we increase the noise in the data, the accuracy of retrieving the order by the Jaccard distance will degrade, but it should still perform relatively well (assuming that the noise is limited). We expect that no rule can provide accuracy of 1, if some noise is introduced.

Q: How we have chosen the values of radii in experiments in Section 6.2, and how would the results look for different values?

A: We have checked different values here, and the results are more or less consistent. The only important variable is that there need to exist a significant variance in radii for the pathological behaviour of the Hamming and Jaccard distance to become visible. The values should also not be too big or too small in order to avoid full votes as well as full empty votes or voters whose approval set do intersect with any other vote. The particular values we have chosen for the paper are mainly dictated by the visualisation quality.

summary.value: This paper lists properties (also called axioms) that uniquely characterize Hamming and Jaccard distances (popular measures for comparing binary vectors). They also propose modifications of these distances called geometric/quadratic Hamming/Jaccad. The authors conduct experiments on synthetic and real data aimed at comparing distance measures.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths:**
- There is a theoretical analysis that describes two popular measures by their properties. This analysis helps to better understand and compare the measures.
- The task of empirically comparing measures is, in general, non-trivial, and the authors propose several experiments aiming at such a comparison.
- The paper is, in general, well written.

**Weaknesses (see details below):**
- Some relevant literature is missing.
- Popular measures are known to have certain biases, which are not discussed.
- There are many other measures that can be analyzed, some of them having better theoretical properties.
- Not all properties are well-motivated.

**Detailed feedback**

**Related literature on evaluating classification performance measures.** 
Distance measures for binary vectors are essentially performance measures for binary classification. In particular, given the anonymity axiom, distance measures are expressed in terms of the entries of the 2x2 confusion matrix. There is a paper by Gösgens et al. (2021) that proposes an axiomatic approach for classification performance measures (binary and multiclass). This work, while being relevant and analyzing some of the listed properties, is not discussed in the current paper.

*M. Gösgens et al. “Good classification measures and how to find them.” NeurIPS 2021.*

**Proposed axioms.** 
Some of the proposed axioms were discussed in Gösgens et al. (2021), while others are not well motivated. Thus, using the term “axiom” instead of, e.g., “properties” seems to be misleading.
- Anonymity: basically says that a measure is defined by the four entries of the confusion matrix.
- Scaling: similar to *scale-invariance* in Gösgens et al. (2021)
- Independent symmetry: this property is not motivated, it is not clear why one should expect it to hold.
- Zero-one symmetry: also not motivated.
- Convergence: the chosen speed of convergence is not motivated.
- Triangle inequality: somehow similar to *distance* in Gösgens et al. (2021), but without other distance axioms.
- Normalization: similar to *minimal agreement* in Gösgens et al. (2021)

**Constant baseline property.**
An important and long-known shortcoming of both Hamming (*accuracy* for binary classification) and Jaccard is that they are biased, i.e., may have an undesirable behavior when classes are imbalanced. This property is known to be critical for reliable evaluation, but it is not discussed in this paper. Also, there are measures like Matthews correlation coefficient and Cohen’s Kappa that are known to be unbiased.

**Other measures.**
There are many measures that can be applied to the task at hand, but only two are discussed in this paper.

**Experiments.**
I like that there are various experiments allowing one to better understand and compare the measures. I have a couple of questions regarding the experiment in Section 6.2:
- Can it be the case that the obtained results depend on a particular clustering algorithm chosen?
- I see that the results illustrate a clear difference between the measures, but why would one want to cluster a dataset that is uniformly generated and thus is not supposed to contain a cluster structure?

**Minor:**
- Line 64: $z_i = y_i$ should probably be $z_i = y_{i-n}$
- Line 238: should it be $f$ instead of $d$ here?
- Line 317: “As mentioned introduction”

summary.value:
In this paper, the authors show the axiomatic characterization of the Hamming and Jaccard distances. Their results are as follows:
(1) Hamming distance satisfies anonymization, scaling, independent symmetry, 0-1 symmetry, convergence, triangle inequality, normalization, but not add 0.
(2) Hamming distance is the only distance that satisfies anonymization, scaling, independent symmetry, 0-1 symmetry, convergence, triangle inequality, normalization.
(3) Jaccard distance satisfies anonymization, scaling, independent symmetry, convergence, triangle inequality, normalization, and add 0. The distance does not satisfy 0-1 symmetry.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
I recommend a rejection of this paper based on the following reasons:
A. As acknowledged by the authors themselves at Line 122, Contribution (1) is trivial and does not provide a substantial advance.

B. While Contributions (1) and (3) have some relevance to machine learning, I find the motivation and practical applicability of Contribution (2) unconvincing.

C. In my view, Contribution (3) is the most compelling. However, the paper fails to acknowledge a substantial body of prior work on the properties of the Jaccard distance. The omission of these citations raises concerns—whether intentional or not—regarding the completeness of the literature review. For instance, the triangle inequality of the Jaccard (Tanimoto) distance was proven in:

> A.H. Lipkus, A proof of the triangle inequality for the Tanimoto distance, J. Math. Chem., 26(1), 1999, pp. 263–265.

Related work on dissimilarity measures includes:

> A. Gragera and V. Suppakitpaisarn, Relaxed triangle inequality ratio of the Sørensen–Dice and Tversky indexes, Theoretical Computer Science, 718, 2018, pp. 37–45.

> T. Itoh and Y. Takei, On Aggregating Two Metrics with Relaxed Triangle Inequalities by the Weighted Harmonic Mean, IEICE Transactions on Fundamentals, Vol. E101-A, No. 9, pp. 1404–1411.

D. I was unable to locate the formal statement of Theorem 4.2 in either the main text or the appendix. Given that Theorem 4.2 appears to be a central contribution of the paper, its omission suggests a lack of thorough proofreading prior to submission.

Minor Comment

Line 863: The inequality should be $J(x, z) \leq$, not $J(x, z) \leftarrow$.

summary.value:
This paper studies the axiomatic characterization of distance metrics for binary vectors, represented by the Hamming and Jaccard distances. The Hamming distance is minimally characterized by Anonymity, Scaling, Independence Symmetry, 0-1 Symmetry, Convergence, Triangle Inequality, and Normalization, while the Jaccard distance is by the same set of axioms except for 0-1 Symmetry being replaced with Add-Zero. This is the first contribution.

Moreover, a pitfall of the axiom Independence Symmetry is pointed out, which is inappropriate when we want to assess the inclusion relationship between two binary vectors. By replacing the arithmetic mean included in the Hamming and Jaccard distances with the geometric mean (and its generalization), the authors propose a p-Hamming and p-Jaccard distances.

In the experiments, the authors investigate (1) how distance metrics well align 1-D and 2-D geometry (2) whether distance metrics yield a visually reasonable cluster structures and (3) whether distance metrics are amenable to real-world label structures. To this end, the geometric Jaccard distance (p=0) looks work well in all scenarios. This fact validates the benefit to deviate from Independence Symmetry.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**

This paper is well-motivated and written nicely. Usually the principled design of distance metrics is not straightforward, and I believe this paper paves a way towards it. We can have a better understanding of what properties these common distances like Hamming and Jaccard do entail. These are good enough reasons for accepting this paper.

**Weaknesses**

Basically I don't think this paper has significant flaws and weaknesses. Just for suggestions, I'd like to raise a few points.

+ Can you discuss whether generalized p-Hamming and p-Jaccard distances preserve the other axioms than Independence Symmetry?
+ Discussing other popular distances such as Dice index, Tversky index, and Sympson's overlap coefficient looks nice. Do they satisfy any of the axioms in Table 1? This comparison should give us better highlights on different metrics.

Very minor points:

+ l227: The first "d" in "d-dimensional" should be italicized.
+ l238: The symbol "d" conflicts with the dimension.

final_justification.value: As stated in the initial review, the axiomatic study of performance metrics is an appealing direction. Though I did not have critical concerns, the authors have adequately responded my comments. After looking at other reviewers' feedback, I feel I'm not catching up all the related literature, and hence I lowered my confidence score from 4 to 3. Nevertheless the rating is kept at 5 just because the contribution remains to be valuable.

title.value: Axiomatic Characterization of the Hamming and Jaccard Distances

TLDR.value: We characterize the Hamming and Jaccard distances using a comprehensive axiom system, which highlights their similarities and differences and identifies their shortcomings.

abstract.value: Measures of dissimilarity between a pair of objects can play a pivotal role in many machine learning objectives such as clustering, outlier detection, or data visualization. In this paper, we focus on data in the form of binary vectors and analyze several methods of measuring dissimilarity between them. We introduce several properties, *axioms*, that a measure of dissimilarity can satisfy and characterize the *Hamming* and *Jaccard* distances as the only measures satisfying particular subsets of our axioms. Based on our analysis, we identify shortcomings of both distances and propose novel approaches that are better suited for certain applications. We complement our theoretical findings by an extensive empirical study. Our primary motivation is the analysis of election data, in which the votes have the form of binary approval of alternatives, but the applicability of our results reaches far beyond that.
